fields.meta_title: File Management Automation for Shared Drives | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build file management automation that renames uploads, files them by client or project, holds duplicates, and archives closed jobs. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build File Management Automation That Files Every Upload
fields.hero_description: Build file management automation that renames each upload, files it in the right folder, and logs each move in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: The Rules Behind Every File Move
fields.features_subheading: Shared drives fill up with files named scan0042 and final-v3. The app you build with Emergent names and files each one by rule.
fields.feature_1:
A naming pattern for every file

Write the convention once, such as CLIENT_DocType_YYYY-MM. The app renames each new file to match it, and the log keeps each file's original name beside the one it now carries.
fields.feature_2:
Every file sent to its folder

Say where each kind of file belongs. A file moves to its folder as soon as a rule matches it, and a file that matches no rule stays in intake with a named owner who places it.
fields.feature_3:
AI that reads what a file is

An AI step reads each upload and pulls fields such as the client, document type, and statement month. A person checks any field the AI is unsure of before the file is renamed.
fields.feature_4:
Changes picked up as they happen

Through your storage service's API, the app runs its rules each time a file is added or changed. A scan that lands in intake at 2 AM has its new name and folder by morning.
fields.feature_5:
A log of every rename and move

Every rename or move is one row: the old path beside the new one, the rule that fired, and the time. The log sits in a database you own. Finding a lost file takes one search.
fields.feature_6:
Your file app's code, in your GitHub

Export the file app's full code to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Your IT team can read each rule that renames or moves a file before that rule runs on a shared drive.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Shared Folders, Each With Its Own Rules
fields.tab_content_1:
Fenwick's scan0042.pdf moves from intake into 2026

Bramwell and Tosh CPAs gets 14 uploads in its client intake folder. The AI step reads Odalys Fenwick's scan0042.pdf as a March 2026 bank statement and files it in Clients/Fenwick/2026 as FENWICK_BankStatement_2026-03.pdf. The app files 12 this way, and 2 it cannot read with confidence wait for Ilse Marchbanks.
fields.tab_content_2:
When project 2611 is won, its 5 folders appear

Quenby Ashworth Architects starts each project from one folder template. When project 2611, Harlow Library, moves to Won in the CRM, the app creates its folder with 5 subfolders: Contracts, Drawings, Consultants, Site Photos, and Invoices. Project lead Ruairi Okonjo gets a direct message with the link.
fields.tab_content_3:
Its checksum matches spring-hero.png, so it waits

Sunniva Ekwueme exports a hero image for Larchfield Creative's brand library and uploads it as hero-final-v3.png. Its checksum matches spring-hero.png, already stored in Brand/2026. The app holds the upload instead of saving a second copy, and Sunniva gets a direct message: keep both, or use the existing file.
fields.tab_content_4:
7 closed jobs move to Archive on the 1st

On the 1st of each month, Dunmore Build Co. runs its archive rule on the Jobs folder. This month it finds 9 closed job folders with no file changed in 24 months. The app moves 7 to Archive and leaves the 2 tagged Warranty open in place. Office manager Celestine Abara gets an email listing all 9 and where each went.

fields.howto_title: How to Build File Management Automation
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to write the naming and filing rules for file management automation, then build and test it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Give each file type a home
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Decide what counts as a duplicate
fields.howto_step_1_des: Open three folders your team uses every day and list how files get there: client uploads, email attachments, and exports from other tools. Copy down the names people give them now, such as scan0042 or final-v3. Start the rules from those real examples.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write the naming convention as a pattern with fixed parts, such as CLIENT_DocType_YYYY-MM. Choose one date format for every rule, and put the year before the month so that names sort by date in any folder list.
fields.howto_step_3_des: For each document type, name the folder it belongs in, such as Clients, then the client, then the year. Decide what happens to a file that no rule matches: leave it in intake and name the person who places it by hand.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Choose how the app spots a copy. A matching name misses a renamed copy, while a checksum compares content. In Google Drive, the MD5 checksum applies only to files with binary content. Plan another test for files without one.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Write which folders the archive rule covers, how long a folder must sit unchanged before it moves, and which tags keep it in place, such as Warranty open. Have the app move old folders to an archive instead of deleting them.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Describe the app in a prompt
fields.howto_step_6_des: Open Emergent and describe the automation in plain English: the folders from step 1, the pattern from step 2, and the duplicate and archive rules you wrote after them. Emergent builds the app and its log from that prompt.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Test on copies, then go live
fields.howto_step_7_des: Point the app at a test folder first, filled with 20 real files copied from intake. Check each new name and location in the log, then connect the live shared drive through its API. Change any rule later by prompting.

faq_plan.a: File management automation is software that names and files documents by rules instead of by hand. A rule watches a folder and reads each new file's name or content. Then it acts: a scan becomes a named statement in the client's folder, and a closed job moves to Archive.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up file management automation?
faq_plan.a: Start from the folders where files land and the names your team gives them today. Write the naming pattern, the folder each file type belongs in, and the rules for duplicates and old work. Then describe all of it to Emergent's AI automation builder, which builds the app from that prompt. Test it on copied files before it touches the live drive.

faq_plan.q: What actions can file management automation run on a shared drive?
faq_plan.a: It can create folders, rename files, and move them, through the storage service's API. In Google Drive, a folder is itself a file with the MIME type application/vnd.google-apps.folder, and the API moves a file between folders with the addParents and removeParents query parameters. A rule calls those operations each time a file matches it.

faq_plan.q: How does file management automation file proposals by client?
faq_plan.a: It gives every sent proposal one naming pattern and one home, such as the client's folder for that year, and a rule files each new version as it is saved. If drafting the document is the slow part, proposal automation covers that job. Keep the pattern short enough to read in a folder list.

faq_plan.q: How does AI file management automation decide which folder a file belongs in?
faq_plan.a: It reads the file's content, not only its name, and pulls out fields such as the client, the document type, and the month. A rule then maps those fields to a folder and a file name. In an app built with Emergent, the AI step sends low-confidence fields to a person, and the file waits in intake until they confirm.

faq_plan.q: Can file management automation find duplicate files that have different names?
faq_plan.a: It can when the rules compare content checksums instead of names. Google Drive's API gives an MD5 checksum for the content of each file with binary content stored in Drive. Dropbox's content_hash lets an app compare remote files to local files without downloading them. Hold any upload whose checksum matches a stored file, and let a person choose which copy to keep.

faq_plan.q: Can file management automation sort the images for each newsletter issue?
faq_plan.a: Yes, when a rule keys on the issue. It can create a folder for each issue, such as 2026-11 Issue, and file every image tagged with that issue into it, renamed by a pattern. Sending the issue is a separate job that newsletter automation covers. With no task cap on automation in Emergent, the rule runs on every upload.

faq_plan.q: Does building file management automation take code?
faq_plan.a: No. Emergent writes the whole app, database included, from a plain-English prompt. To change a rule, describe the change in a new prompt. The free tier covers building and publishing.

faq_plan.q: When does file management automation run after a new file is uploaded?
faq_plan.a: It runs when the storage service reports the change. The Google Drive API sends a notification message as a POST request to a set URL whenever a watched resource changes. Microsoft Graph offers a delta call that tracks changes in a drive item and its children over time, and its docs say to track items by id.

faq_plan.q: Should a scanned batch be split before file management automation renames it?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Write naming and filing rules for one document per file: split a multi-document scan first, then let each piece pick up its own name and folder. Splitting and merging scans is the job pdf automation handles, and the rules on this page take over once each file stands alone.

plan.angle: The live top 10 for file management automation is desktop organizers (rule-based sorting of a Downloads folder on one Mac or PC), an app directory and software roundups; none shows rules running on a team's shared storage. This page shows file management automation as one app that watches shared folders: it names each upload by a convention, files it under the right client or project, creates a project's folder tree when the deal is won, holds a duplicate by comparing checksums, and moves closed jobs to an archive on a schedule, with every move logged in a database the user owns. It stays off generating document content (the document automation page) and splitting, merging or filling PDFs (the pdf automation page).
